(Hint: you may assume the MLE is asymptotically efficient.)

## Setup and notation

Let the true parameter be \(\theta_0\in\Theta\subset\mathbb R^d\), with \(\theta_0\) an interior point. Write

\[
L_n(\theta)=\prod_{i=1}^n p_\theta(X_i),\qquad 
\ell_n^{\log}(\theta)=\log L_n(\theta),
\]

and the negative log-likelihood as

\[
l_n(\theta)=-\ell_n^{\log}(\theta).
\]

Let

\[
S_n(\theta)=\nabla_\theta \ell_n^{\log}(\theta)=-\nabla l_n(\theta)
\]

be the score, and let

\[
H_n(\theta)=\nabla^2 l_n(\theta)
\]

be the Hessian of the negative log-likelihood. The Fisher information for one observation is

\[
I(\theta)=\mathbb E_\theta\big[s_\theta(X)s_\theta(X)^\top\big],
\qquad s_\theta(X)=\nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(X),
\]

and for the full sample,

\[
I_n(\theta)=\mathbb E_\theta\big[S_n(\theta)S_n(\theta)^\top\big]=nI(\theta).
\]

Assume \(I(\theta)\) is nonsingular.

---

# (i) Cramér–Rao lower bound

Let \(\psi:\Theta\to\mathbb R^q\) be differentiable, and let \(T=T(X_1,\dots,X_n)\in\mathbb R^q\) be unbiased for \(\psi(\theta)\), i.e.

\[
\mathbb E_\theta[T]=\psi(\theta).
\]

Let

\[
D\psi(\theta)=\frac{\partial \psi(\theta)}{\partial \theta^\top}
\]

denote the \(q\times d\) Jacobian matrix. Then the multivariate Cramér–Rao lower bound is

\[
\boxed{
\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(T)\succeq D\psi(\theta)\, I_n(\theta)^{-1}\, D\psi(\theta)^\top
}
\]

or, equivalently, since \(I_n(\theta)=nI(\theta)\),

\[
\boxed{
\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(T)\succeq \frac1n D\psi(\theta)\, I(\theta)^{-1}\, D\psi(\theta)^\top .
}
\]

For scalar \(\psi\), this becomes

\[
\boxed{
\operatorname{Var}_\theta(T)\ge \frac1n \nabla \psi(\theta)^\top I(\theta)^{-1}\nabla \psi(\theta).
}
\]

## Proof

Let \(f_\theta^{(n)}(x_1,\dots,x_n)=\prod_{i=1}^n p_\theta(x_i)\) be the joint density. Under the stated regularity conditions, differentiation under the integral sign is valid.

First,

\[
\mathbb E_\theta[S_n(\theta)]
=
\int \nabla_\theta \log f_\theta^{(n)}(x)\, f_\theta^{(n)}(x)\,dx
=
\int \nabla_\theta f_\theta^{(n)}(x)\,dx
=
\nabla_\theta \int f_\theta^{(n)}(x)\,dx
=0.
\]

Next, since \(T\) is unbiased,

\[
\psi(\theta)=\mathbb E_\theta[T].
\]

Differentiating both sides gives

\[
D\psi(\theta)
=
\nabla_\theta \mathbb E_\theta[T]
=
\int T(x)\, \nabla_\theta f_\theta^{(n)}(x)^\top dx.
\]

Because

\[
\nabla_\theta f_\theta^{(n)}(x)
=
f_\theta^{(n)}(x)\, S_n(\theta),
\]

we get

\[
D\psi(\theta)
=
\mathbb E_\theta\big[T S_n(\theta)^\top\big].
\]

Using \(\mathbb E_\theta[S_n(\theta)]=0\), this is

\[
D\psi(\theta)
=
\mathbb E_\theta\big[(T-\psi(\theta))S_n(\theta)^\top\big].
\]

Now define

\[
A=T-\psi(\theta),\qquad S=S_n(\theta).
\]

Then

\[
\mathbb E_\theta[AS^\top]=D\psi(\theta),
\qquad 
\mathbb E_\theta[SS^\top]=I_n(\theta).
\]

Consider the random vector

\[
U=A-D\psi(\theta) I_n(\theta)^{-1} S.
\]

Since covariance matrices are positive semidefinite,

\[
\mathbb E_\theta[UU^\top]\succeq 0.
\]

Expanding,

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E_\theta[UU^\top]
&=
\mathbb E_\theta[AA^\top]
-
D\psi I_n^{-1}\mathbb E_\theta[SA^\top]
-
\mathbb E_\theta[AS^\top]I_n^{-1}D\psi^\top
+
D\psi I_n^{-1}\mathbb E_\theta[SS^\top]I_n^{-1}D\psi^\top \\
&=
\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(T)
-
D\psi I_n^{-1}D\psi^\top
-
D\psi I_n^{-1}D\psi^\top
+
D\psi I_n^{-1}I_n I_n^{-1}D\psi^\top \\
&=
\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(T)
-
D\psi I_n^{-1}D\psi^\top.
\end{aligned}
\]

Therefore

\[
\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(T)-D\psi(\theta)I_n(\theta)^{-1}D\psi(\theta)^\top\succeq 0.
\]

This proves the Cramér–Rao lower bound.

---

# (ii) One-step Newton–Raphson estimator and asymptotic efficiency

Let \(\tilde\theta\) be an initial estimator satisfying

\[
\|\tilde\theta-\theta_0\|_2=o_p(n^{-1/4}).
\]

Define the normalized Hessian

\[
A_n(\theta)=\frac1n H_n(\theta),
\]

and the normalized gradient

\[
g_n(\theta)=\frac1n \nabla l_n(\theta).
\]

The Newton–Raphson one-step estimator is

\[
\boxed{
\hat\theta
=
\tilde\theta
-
H_n(\tilde\theta)^{-1}\nabla l_n(\tilde\theta)
}
\]

or equivalently,

\[
\boxed{
\hat\theta
=
\tilde\theta
-
A_n(\tilde\theta)^{-1} g_n(\tilde\theta).
}
\]

We will show that

\[
\sqrt n(\hat\theta-\theta_0)
\Rightarrow
N\bigl(0,I(\theta_0)^{-1}\bigr),
\]

and hence \(\hat\theta\) is asymptotically efficient.

Let \(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}}\) denote the MLE. By the hint, we may assume the MLE is asymptotically efficient, so

\[
\sqrt n(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}}-\theta_0)
\Rightarrow
N\bigl(0,I(\theta_0)^{-1}\bigr).
\]

It suffices to prove that

\[
\hat\theta-\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}}=o_p(n^{-1/2}).
\]

Indeed, then Slutsky’s theorem gives the desired asymptotic normality.

---

## Step 1: Invertibility of the Hessian at \(\tilde\theta\)

By regularity,

\[
A_n(\theta_0)=\frac1n H_n(\theta_0)\overset{p}\longrightarrow I(\theta_0).
\]

Since \(I(\theta_0)\) is positive definite, let

\[
\lambda_{\min}(I(\theta_0))>0.
\]

Also \(\tilde\theta\to_p\theta_0\), because \(o_p(n^{-1/4})=o_p(1)\). Using the Lipschitz condition on the Hessian, in normalized form,

\[
\|A_n(\tilde\theta)-A_n(\theta_0)\|
\le L\|\tilde\theta-\theta_0\|
=o_p(1).
\]

Therefore

\[
A_n(\tilde\theta)\overset{p}\longrightarrow I(\theta_0).
\]

Hence, with probability tending to one, \(A_n(\tilde\theta)\) is nonsingular and

\[
\|A_n(\tilde\theta)^{-1}\|=O_p(1).
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\|H_n(\tilde\theta)^{-1}\|=O_p(n^{-1}).
\]

---

## Step 2: Taylor expansion around \(\tilde\theta\)

Because \(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}}\) satisfies the likelihood equation,

\[
\nabla l_n(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}})=0,
\]

or equivalently,

\[
g_n(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}})=0.
\]

Let

\[
d_n=\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}}-\tilde\theta.
\]

Since

\[
\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}}-\theta_0=O_p(n^{-1/2})
\]

and

\[
\tilde\theta-\theta_0=o_p(n^{-1/4}),
\]

we have

\[
d_n
=
\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}}-\tilde\theta
=
O_p(n^{-1/2})+o_p(n^{-1/4})
=
o_p(n^{-1/4}).
\]

Now Taylor expand \(g_n\) around \(\tilde\theta\):

\[
0
=
g_n(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}})
=
g_n(\tilde\theta)
+
A_n(\tilde\theta)d_n
+
r_n,
\]

where the integral remainder is

\[
r_n
=
\int_0^1
\left[
A_n(\tilde\theta+t d_n)-A_n(\tilde\theta)
\right]d_n\,dt.
\]

Using the Lipschitz condition,

\[
\begin{aligned}
\|r_n\|
&\le
\int_0^1
\|A_n(\tilde\theta+t d_n)-A_n(\tilde\theta)\|
\|d_n\|\,dt \\
&\le
\int_0^1 L t\|d_n\|^2\,dt \\
&=
\frac L2 \|d_n\|^2.
\end{aligned}
\]

Since \(d_n=o_p(n^{-1/4})\),

\[
\|d_n\|^2=o_p(n^{-1/2}),
\]

so

\[
r_n=o_p(n^{-1/2}).
\]

From the Taylor expansion,

\[
g_n(\tilde\theta)
=
-A_n(\tilde\theta)d_n-r_n.
\]

Therefore the one-step estimator satisfies

\[
\begin{aligned}
\hat\theta
&=
\tilde\theta
-
A_n(\tilde\theta)^{-1}g_n(\tilde\theta) \\
&=
\tilde\theta
+
d_n
+
A_n(\tilde\theta)^{-1}r_n \\
&=
\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}}
+
A_n(\tilde\theta)^{-1}r_n.
\end{aligned}
\]

Hence

\[
\|\hat\theta-\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}}\|
\le
\|A_n(\tilde\theta)^{-1}\|\|r_n\|
=
O_p(1)\, o_p(n^{-1/2})
=
o_p(n^{-1/2}).
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{
\hat\theta-\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}}=o_p(n^{-1/2}).
}
\]

---

## Step 3: Asymptotic normality

Since

\[
\sqrt n(\hat\theta-\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}})=o_p(1),
\]

and

\[
\sqrt n(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}}-\theta_0)
\Rightarrow
N\bigl(0,I(\theta_0)^{-1}\bigr),
\]

Slutsky’s theorem implies

\[
\boxed{
\sqrt n(\hat\theta-\theta_0)
\Rightarrow
N\bigl(0,I(\theta_0)^{-1}\bigr).
}
\]

Equivalently, the one-step estimator has the same first-order asymptotic distribution as the MLE.

---

## Step 4: Achieving the Cramér–Rao lower bound

For estimating \(\theta\) itself, take \(\psi(\theta)=\theta\). Then \(D\psi(\theta)=I_d\), and the Cramér–Rao lower bound from part (i) is

\[
\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(T)\succeq I_n(\theta)^{-1}
=
\frac1n I(\theta)^{-1}.
\]

The one-step estimator satisfies

\[
\sqrt n(\hat\theta-\theta_0)
\Rightarrow
N\bigl(0,I(\theta_0)^{-1}\bigr),
\]

so its asymptotic covariance is

\[
\frac1n I(\theta_0)^{-1},
\]

which equals the Cramér–Rao lower bound to first order. Hence \(\hat\theta\) is asymptotically efficient.

For a general differentiable functional \(\psi(\theta)\), define the plug-in estimator

\[
\hat\psi=\psi(\hat\theta).
\]

By the delta method,

\[
\sqrt n\bigl(\hat\psi-\psi(\theta_0)\bigr)
\Rightarrow
N\left(
0,\,
D\psi(\theta_0)I(\theta_0)^{-1}D\psi(\theta_0)^\top
\right).
\]

But the Cramér–Rao lower bound for unbiased estimators of \(\psi(\theta)\) is

\[
\frac1n
D\psi(\theta_0)I(\theta_0)^{-1}D\psi(\theta_0)^\top.
\]

Therefore \(\psi(\hat\theta)\) also achieves the Cramér–Rao lower bound asymptotically.

Thus,

\[
\boxed{
\hat\theta
=
\tilde\theta
-
H_n(\tilde\theta)^{-1}\nabla l_n(\tilde\theta)
}
\]

is asymptotically normal and asymptotically efficient.
